findings.detail: The function docstring states that an empty quantity "is already reported as 'Missing Qty for Ingredient' earlier in the validation pass". That block lives inside `if (strictEmptyCheck)` at components/CompositeTab.tsx:506, and the call site's truthiness guard at CompositeTab.tsx:554 means `classifyQuantity` never sees the blank either. With the toggle off, a blank quantity is reported by nothing. CompositeTab's own comment (lines 546-553) states this caveat explicitly and calls it a deliberate product decision; the util's docstring — which is what a second caller will read — presents the blank path as unconditionally covered. Nothing is broken today (a blank reaching the function still returns `non-numeric`), but the docstring is the artifact that would let the next caller omit its own blank handling on a false premise.
findings.summary: Docstring says blank is "already reported" — true only when Strict Empty Check is on

findings.detail: The § "Confirmed defects" section lists four defects: (1) preview vs export, (2) dates as serials, (3) header-styling crash, (4) error cells matching the wrong row. The sentence above them claims all four are registered as TD-043/TD-044/TD-045/TD-046 — but TD-044 is "Smart Lookup has no tests", which is not one of those four, and defect #4 (error cells, also parity-table row 7, P2) has no entry in docs/quality/tech-debt-register.md at all. I checked the register: TD-043 is preview/export, TD-045 is dates, TD-046 is the empty-header crash, and nothing covers error-cell keys. So a defect this PR documents as confirmed is simultaneously asserted to be tracked and is not — which is precisely the silent-debt case the technical-debt handbook exists to catch, made worse because the sentence tells a future reader not to look.
findings.summary: "All four are registered" mismaps the defect list — the error-cell defect is untracked

findings.detail: `expect(performance.now() - started).toBeLessThan(1_000)` is a timing assertion, and the repo already carries TD-040 for intermittent, timing-shaped failures that block pushes. I am NOT calling this a defect: the regex is linear on this input, so the real runtime is single-digit milliseconds and the 1 s bound leaves roughly two orders of magnitude of headroom — the guard is well-calibrated and catches the quadratic form it exists to catch. Recording it only so the pattern is a deliberate choice: if this ever does fail on a loaded CI worker, the failure will look like a regex regression rather than scheduler noise, and the next reader will spend time on the wrong hypothesis.
findings.summary: Wall-clock assertion couples the ReDoS guard test to machine speed
